unit-m1r.srcName: enVision Math G4, Topic 1 (HW 1-1 to 1-5, Drive)

summary.text: A review pool for all of Topic 1 (lessons 1-1 through 1-5): place value and periods, the ten-times relationship, word and expanded forms, comparing and ordering, rounding to any place, rounding neighbourhoods, and constructing arguments with counterexamples.

why.text: The end-of-topic test mixes every lesson together, so practice should too. A 12-question sitting drawn from a 24-question pool means two passes cover everything — and the mix itself is the practice, because deciding WHICH skill a question wants is half the test.

objectives.text: Read, write, compare and round numbers through one million
Reason about rounding neighbourhoods in both directions

parentNote.text: A review pool, not a lesson: 24 fresh questions across all five Topic 1 lessons, served 12 per sitting with flashcards that recap each big idea. Approve it when the class heads into review days before the Topic 1 test. Two sittings cover the pool; questions she misses go to the Growth Zone ladder like always. The word-problem and argument questions deliberately mirror the test's explain-your-reasoning style.

nextUp.text: Twelve questions per sitting — a fuller round, like the real test. Two sittings covers the pool.

cards.def:
**A big number reads in three-digit chunks called periods, separated by commas.**
• 415,203: the thousands period says 415, the ones period says 203.
• Read the chunk, say the period's name, move right.

**A digit one place to the left is worth ten times as much.**
• In 66,000 the left 6 is 60,000 and the right 6 is 6,000.
• Same digit, different address, ten times the value.

**Compare from the LEFT, place by place; the first difference decides.**
• More digits wins outright — 102,003 beats 98,764 before any marching.
• Digits after the deciding place never get a vote.

**Find the rounding place, look one digit right: 5 or more rounds up. Zero out the rest.**
• 68,341 to the nearest thousand: the 3 says stay — 68,000.
• The number line's halfway point says the same thing, slower and surer.

**Every benchmark owns a range: from its halfway point below to just under its halfway point above.**
• 60,000 (nearest ten thousand) collects everything from 55,000 through 64,999.
• You cannot un-round — the original is a range, not a number.
cards.hint: A rounded number is a neighbourhood, not an address.

cards.def:
**Translate one period at a time; missing places fill with zeros.**
• "Two hundred five thousand, sixty" → 205,—, then 060: 205,060.
• Most wrong arguments about big numbers begin with a wrong translation.

**A math argument names its deciding place; one counterexample kills an always-claim.**
• "Because it looks bigger" is a feeling. "The hundreds differ: 2 > 0" is an argument.
• To break "always", find one case that fails — that is a complete proof.

questions.q: What is the value of the 7 in 738,251?
questions.hint: Name the place before naming the value.
steps: The 7 sits in the hundred thousands place.
Its value is 7 × 100,000.
So the 7 is worth 700,000.

ex.main: **700,000.** The digit is 7; the place multiplies it by one hundred thousand.
ex.tip: Digit and value are different questions. The place is what turns one into the other.

questions.q: Write "two hundred five thousand, sixty" as a number.
questions.hint: One period at a time — and let zeros hold the empty places.
steps: "Two hundred five thousand" fills the thousands period: 205,—.
"Sixty" fills the ones period as 060.
Together: 205,060.

ex.main: **205,060.** The words skipped the hundreds and the ones, so zeros hold those seats.
ex.tip: The comma you hear in the words is the comma you write in the number.

questions.q: Which is the expanded form of 480,209?
questions.hint: Every nonzero digit contributes its place value.
steps: 4 is in the hundred thousands: 400,000.
8 is in the ten thousands: 80,000.
2 is in the hundreds: 200, and 9 is in the ones: 9.
The zeros in the thousands and tens contribute nothing to write.

ex.main: **400,000 + 80,000 + 200 + 9.** Expanded form is the number confessing what each digit is worth.
ex.tip: Zeros appear in standard form but vanish in expanded form — they hold places, not value.

questions.q: In 66,000, how does the value of the left 6 compare to the right 6?
opts: It is ten times as much — 60,000 against 6,000
They are equal — the digit is the same
It is one hundred times as much
It is six times as much
questions.hint: Same digit, neighbouring places.
steps: The left 6 is in the ten thousands: 60,000.
The right 6 is in the thousands: 6,000.
One step left multiplies a digit's value by ten.

ex.main: **Ten times as much.** Place, not the digit itself, sets the value.
ex.tip: This is THE place-value relationship — every column is worth ten of the one to its right.

questions.q: Compare: 372,845 ▢ 372,899. Which symbol, and which place decides?
opts: < — the tens differ: 4 tens against 9 tens
> — 845 has a bigger hundreds digit
= — the first four digits match
< — the ones decide it
questions.hint: March from the left until the digits disagree.
steps: Hundred thousands, ten thousands, thousands, hundreds: 3, 7, 2, 8 — all match.
Tens: 4 against 9. First difference.

ex.main: **< , decided at the tens.** Every place before it agreed, so the tens got the vote.
ex.tip: Name the deciding place in every comparison — that is the argument, not just the answer.

questions.q: Round 68,341 to the nearest thousand.
questions.hint: One digit right of the thousands place makes the call.
steps: The rounding place is the thousands: the 8.
One digit right: 3. Less than 5, so the 8 stays.
Zero out the rest: 68,000.

ex.main: **68,000.** The 341 tail is below the halfway point, so the number settles down.
ex.tip: Rounding looks at ONE digit. Everything past it is already decided.

questions.q: Round 452,616 to the nearest hundred thousand.
questions.hint: The ten thousands digit decides.
steps: The rounding place is the hundred thousands: the 4.
One digit right: 5. Five or more rounds up.
The 4 becomes 5, the rest zero out: 500,000.

ex.main: **500,000.** The 5 in the ten thousands is exactly enough to push it up.
ex.tip: At the school rule, 5 always rounds up — no coin flips, no exceptions.

questions.q: What is the halfway point between 23,000 and 24,000?
questions.hint: Half of the gap, added to the lower benchmark.
steps: The gap between the benchmarks is 1,000.
Half of 1,000 is 500.

ex.main: **23,500.** Below it rounds down; at or above it rounds up.
ex.tip: Halfway points end in 5-then-zeros. Spot the shape and you can write them instantly.

questions.q: The comma in 415,203 separates which two things?
opts: The thousands period from the ones period
The big digits from the small ones
The even places from the odd places
Nothing — it is decoration
questions.hint: Commas mark off three-digit reading chunks.
steps: 415,203 reads as two chunks: 415 and 203.
The left chunk is the thousands period: "four hundred fifteen thousand".
The right chunk is the ones period: "two hundred three".

ex.main: **The thousands period from the ones period.** The comma is where you say the word "thousand".
ex.tip: Reading big numbers is chunking. The commas are the chunk boundaries, printed.

questions.q: In which number is the 5 worth exactly 50,000?
questions.hint: Find where each 5 lives before judging its worth.
steps: 352,610: the 5 sits in the ten thousands — worth 50,000.
35,261: that 5 is in the thousands — 5,000.
523,000: hundred thousands — 500,000. And 3,520: hundreds — 500.

ex.main: **352,610.** Only there does the 5 occupy the ten thousands seat.
ex.tip: Same digit, four different values. The address does all the work.

questions.q: Order these from least to greatest: 89,420 · 89,204 · 98,024.
questions.hint: Compare pairs with the left-to-right march.
steps: 98,024 starts with 9 ten thousands — it beats both 8-starters. Greatest.
Between 89,420 and 89,204: ten thousands and thousands match; hundreds 4 against 2.
89,204 has the smaller hundreds, so it is least: 89,204 < 89,420 < 98,024.

ex.main: **89,204 < 89,420 < 98,024.** One march settled the twins; the digit count settled the third.
ex.tip: Ordering is just comparison run twice. Do the easy elimination first.

questions.q: What number is ten times 8,700?
questions.hint: Ten times means every digit moves one place left.
steps: Ten times a number shifts each digit one place left.
8 thousands become 8 ten thousands; 7 hundreds become 7 thousands.

ex.main: **87,000.** The digits kept their order and moved up one address each.
ex.tip: Multiplying by ten never changes the digits — only their places.

questions.q: What is the SMALLEST number that rounds to 60,000 at the nearest ten thousand?
questions.hint: The bottom of the neighbourhood is the halfway point below.
steps: Numbers reach 60,000 from below starting at the halfway point.
Halfway between 50,000 and 60,000 is 55,000 — and 5 rounds up.
So 55,000 is the smallest; 54,999 drops to 50,000 instead.

ex.main: **55,000.** The neighbourhood of 60,000 runs from 55,000 through 64,999.
ex.tip: Smallest-possible questions always land ON the halfway point. Largest-possible land just under the next one.

questions.q: What is the LARGEST number that rounds to 341,000 at the nearest thousand?
questions.hint: Just under the halfway point above.
steps: The next benchmark up is 342,000; the halfway point is 341,500.
At 341,500 the school rule says round UP — too far.
One less, 341,499, still rounds down to 341,000. That is the ceiling.

ex.main: **341,499.** The halfway point itself defects to 342,000, so the largest keeper is one below it.
ex.tip: The "largest that rounds to" answer always ends in 499…, one short of the halfway point.

questions.q: A sign says a stadium holds "about 30,000", rounded to the nearest ten thousand. Which could be the exact capacity?
questions.hint: Find the full range that rounds to 30,000 first.
steps: The 30,000 neighbourhood runs from 25,000 through 34,999.
34,999 is inside it — just barely.

ex.main: **34,999.** Un-rounding gives a range, and this is its very top.
ex.tip: Boundary numbers are where these questions live. Check the edges, not the middle.

questions.q: Compare 98,764 and 102,003. Which is greater, and why?
opts: 102,003 — it has a hundred thousands place and 98,764 does not
98,764 — its digits are bigger
They cannot be compared with different digit counts
questions.hint: Count the digits before comparing any of them.
steps: 98,764 has five digits; 102,003 has six.
A six-digit number has a hundred thousands place — worth more than any five-digit number can reach.
So 102,003 > 98,764, before any digit-by-digit march.

ex.main: **102,003.** More places beats bigger digits, every time.
ex.tip: The 9-beats-1 trap only works on numbers the same length. Length first, march second.

questions.q: Write (3 × 100,000) + (4 × 1,000) + (7 × 10) as a standard number.
questions.hint: Give every unmentioned place a zero.
steps: No ten thousands, no hundreds, no ones — zeros hold those places.

ex.main: **304,070.** Three values, three zeros standing guard between them.
ex.tip: Building from expanded form is a seating chart: every place gets a digit, even if it is 0.

questions.q: Rosa claims: "A number that contains a 9 is always greater than a number with no 9s." Which counterexample breaks it?
opts: 9,999 < 10,000 — the all-9s number loses to one with none
99 > 88, which supports the claim
19 > 12, which supports the claim
No counterexample exists; the claim is true
questions.hint: Hunt for a 9-heavy number that still loses.
steps: 9,999 is nothing but 9s. 10,000 contains none.
But 10,000 has five digits against four — it is greater.
One failing case, claim finished: digit VALUE never beats place count.

ex.main: **9,999 < 10,000.** The claim dies in one line, because places outrank digits.
ex.tip: Supporting examples never prove an always-claim. One counterexample disproves it. Attack is cheaper.

questions.q: Lena rounds 47,562 to the nearest thousand and announces 50,000. What actually happened?
opts: She rounded to the nearest ten thousand — the nearest thousand is 48,000
Nothing; 50,000 is correct
She should have said 47,000
She rounded down instead of up
questions.hint: Check which place her answer is faithful to.
steps: Nearest thousand: rounding digit 7, next digit 5 — round up to 48,000.
50,000 is what the nearest TEN thousand gives (the 7 pushes the 4 up).
Her arithmetic was fine; her place was wrong.

ex.main: **Wrong place — 48,000 was the ask.** A correct rounding of the wrong place is still a wrong answer.
ex.tip: Underline the place word in every rounding question. It is the most commonly dropped word in the topic.

questions.q: To argue 512,006 < 512,600 completely, which sentence chain does it?
opts: The first three places match at 5, 1, 2 — then the hundreds differ: 0 < 6
512,600 simply looks bigger
The ones differ: 6 > 0, so 512,006 is greater
Both have six digits, so they are equal
questions.hint: Anchor the matching places, then name the deciding one.
steps: Hundred thousands, ten thousands, thousands: 5, 1, 2 — identical.
Hundreds: 0 against 6. First difference.
0 hundreds < 6 hundreds settles it; the later digits never vote.
Stating the matches first is what makes the argument checkable.

ex.main: **Match, match, match, then 0 < 6 at the hundreds.** The boring steps are part of the proof.
ex.tip: The ones-place option reaches a wrong verdict from real digits — deciding from the wrong place is the classic broken argument.

questions.q: A sign reads "four hundred sixteen thousand visitors". Rio writes 400,016. Diagnose the translation.
opts: The whole 416 belongs in the thousands period — the number is 416,000
Rio is correct
It should be 400,160
It should be 4,016
questions.hint: Which words live inside the thousands period?
steps: "Four hundred sixteen" is all one chunk, and "thousand" names its period.
So 416 fills the thousands period: 416,000.
Rio split the chunk — he sent 400 to the thousands and 16 to the ones.
The ones period is empty here: no words came after "thousand".

ex.main: **416,000.** Everything before the word "thousand" stays together in that period.
ex.tip: Splitting a period's chunk is the source of most translation errors. The comma in the words marks the only legal cut.

questions.q: Ben claims: "If one number is bigger than another, its rounded value is bigger too." Which counterexample breaks it?
opts: 62 and 58 — 62 > 58, but both round to 60 at the nearest ten
70 and 30 — they round to different numbers
91 > 89, and 90 > 90 fails… so the claim holds
No counterexample exists
questions.hint: Look for two different numbers sharing a rounding neighbourhood.
steps: 62 > 58 — the numbers genuinely differ.
But both live in 60's neighbourhood: each rounds to 60.
"Bigger" promised bigger; equal is not bigger. Claim broken.

ex.main: **62 and 58 both round to 60.** Rounding flattens small differences, so bigger-in, bigger-out fails.
ex.tip: Rounding is many-to-one — that single fact generates most of its counterexamples.

questions.q: A poster says a whale sanctuary hosts 4,120 visitors a day — "about ten times" the 43 daily visitors of a tide-pool exhibit. Test the claim with estimates.
opts: It fails — ten times 43 is about 430; 4,120 is closer to one hundred times
It holds — both numbers are large
It holds — 4,120 contains a 4 and so does 43
It cannot be tested without exact figures
questions.hint: Multiply the small number by ten and compare.
steps: Ten times 43 is 430.
4,120 is nearly ten times THAT — around a hundred times 43.
The estimate alone settles it: the claim overshoots by a factor of ten.

ex.main: **It fails — 430 is ten times 43, and 4,120 is far past it.** Estimates are enough to sink a bad ratio claim.
ex.tip: Times-ten claims are place-value claims: one place left is ×10, two places is ×100. Count the shift.

questions.q: A librarian says the collection holds "about 341,000 books, to the nearest thousand". Could the exact count be 340,512?
opts: Yes — the 5 in the hundreds rounds 340,512 up to 341,000
No — 340,512 rounds to 340,000
Yes — any count starting with 340 works
Yes — rounding does not restrict the count
questions.hint: Round 340,512 to the nearest thousand and see where it lands.
steps: Rounding place: the thousands (the 0 in 340,512).
One digit right: 5 — five or more rounds up.
340,512 → 341,000. It fits the sign after all.

ex.main: **Yes — 340,512 rounds up to 341,000.** The neighbourhood runs 340,500 through 341,499, and it is inside.
ex.tip: Work the rule before trusting your gut — 340,512 FEELS like it belongs to 340,000, and the 5 says otherwise.
